title: Personal Space Between Men
hook: Two men often stand further apart than any other pair, and the gap is rarely about dislike; it is about what closeness might be taken to mean.
why:
Watch men in a queue, at a urinal, on a sofa, in a lift. They space themselves with a precision nobody taught them: the empty seat left between two men at the cinema, the urinal skipped, the far end of the bench. Then watch the same men on a football terrace, in a rugby scrum or at a funeral, pressed together without a second thought. The rules are strict, and they change completely with the setting.

The chapter on proxemics in Part I covered the general science of personal space. This chapter is about what is specific to men with other men: why the gap is often larger, how much of it is fear of being misread, how it is changing between generations, the unwritten rules men keep, the settings that suspend those rules, how to read a change in distance between two men, and how to make room for closeness when it would help.

teach.p:
Observational studies of how people stand and sit, mostly carried out in Western countries, have often found that pairs of men keep more distance from each other than pairs of women do, with mixed pairs somewhere in between. The pattern is not universal, and it varies a great deal with culture, age, setting and relationship. But in many places, two male acquaintances talking at a party stand a little further apart, and angle themselves a little more, than two female acquaintances in the same room.

Why? Biological sex alone seems to be a poor explanation. In a 2006 study, the psychologists Uzzell and Horne measured the distances people kept and also asked about their gender roles, how strongly they identified with traditionally masculine or feminine traits. Gender role turned out to matter more than whether someone was male or female. Distance, in other words, is partly a performance of a certain kind of masculinity.

That matters for a reader. The gap between two men is rarely a measure of how much they like each other. Close friends may still stand further apart than two women who have just met. To read distance between men, compare it with what is normal for those men in that setting, not with what would be normal between other people.

The figures here stand side by side, a comfortable arm's length apart, each with his own space. Nothing in the picture says they are distant. It says they are two men in a culture where this is how two men stand.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men, in a given place, stood as close to each other as women do. In many cultures they do, and the differences found in Western studies vary with setting, which is why distance must be read against local and personal baselines.

teach.h: The fear of what closeness means.
teach.p:
The sociologist Eric Anderson coined a word for one force behind the gap: homohysteria, men's fear of being seen as gay. He argued that when that fear is high in a culture, straight men police their own behaviour and each other's, avoiding closeness, touch and tenderness between men that might be misread. When the fear falls, men have more room.

Anderson and Mark McCormack have described a shift among younger men in Britain and elsewhere. In studies of schools and sports teams, they found boys and young men hugging, leaning on each other, sharing beds on trips and expressing affection to friends in ways that, they argue, would have been unthinkable among straight boys a generation earlier. A study of older British men found many of them looking at this behaviour with disapproval, a reminder that the rules they grew up with were stricter.

This research is mostly qualitative and based on particular groups, so it should not be read as a description of all young men. But it fits what many families notice: sons who hug their friends, and fathers who keep their distance from theirs.

The fear costs everyone. It keeps straight men from comfort they might want, it makes gay men targets, and it turns ordinary closeness between friends into something to be explained or joked away. The figures here sit across a table from each other, at a careful distance. For some men, that table is not furniture but a wall.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men's distance from each other showed no link to cultural attitudes to homosexuality. The evidence for the link is largely qualitative and from particular places, so it is a strong interpretation rather than a measured law.

teach.p:
Men keep a set of spacing rules that are almost never spoken aloud. At a row of urinals, a man will usually choose one that leaves a gap. At the cinema, two male friends often leave an empty seat between them. In a waiting room, men spread out to the ends of benches. In a lift, they redistribute themselves each time someone gets out.

The rules have physical effects. In a 1976 study that has become notorious, Dennis Middlemist and his colleagues measured how long it took men at a university lavatory to begin urinating when another man stood at the next urinal, one urinal away, or not at all. The closer the other man, the longer the delay, which the researchers took as evidence that crowding raises physical arousal.

The study is also taught as a warning. The men were observed in secret, through a periscope in a cubicle, without their consent and without being told afterwards. Critics called it an affront to dignity. For this book, it carries both lessons: closeness between men has measurable effects on the body, and curiosity about other people's bodies has limits that no research question overrides.

When you see a man break one of these rules, choosing the next urinal, the adjacent seat, the middle of the bench, the most likely explanation is ordinary: the place is crowded, or he did not notice, or he does not share the rule. The figures here sit together on a bench. One has taken the end; the other could have taken the other end, and chose not to. Between friends, that choice is small and warm.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men's spacing in places like lavatories and cinemas were random. The pattern is widely observed, and the Middlemist study found physical effects of closeness, though it was small, old and ethically compromised.

teach.p:
The same men who keep a careful gap at a bus stop will stand pressed together on a football terrace, singing. Crowds change the rules, and the chapter on proxemics described how unwelcome crowding, on a packed commuter train, wears on the body. But a crowd you belong to is different.

In 2010 David Novelli, John Drury and Stephen Reicher tested this directly. They put people into groups and then asked them to arrange chairs for a conversation. People placed their chairs closer to someone they had been told was a member of their own group than to someone from another group, or to someone with no group label at all. Personal space, they argued, depends less on how many people are around than on who they are, and on whether we see them as us.

This explains a great deal of men's closeness. Teammates in a huddle, soldiers in a vehicle, fans on a terrace, men at a funeral, bandmates on a stage: in each case a shared identity, often marked by a shared purpose, licenses a closeness that would be uncomfortable between the same men elsewhere. The closeness often goes further: arms around shoulders, heads together, embraces after a goal.

The figures here stand shoulder to shoulder, each with an arm across the other's shoulders. It is a posture men adopt easily in a team photo and rarely on a high street. Same men, same bodies: different us.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people kept the same distance from members of their own group as from outsiders. Novelli and colleagues found that they did not, though in laboratory groups created for the study, so the size of the effect in real crowds may differ.
teach.pullQuote: Same men, same bodies: different us.

teach.h: Shoulder to shoulder, not nose to nose.
teach.p:
Men's distance depends heavily on angle. Two men who would feel uncomfortable standing half a metre apart face to face will stand shoulder to shoulder at a bar, almost touching, for an hour. On a bench, at a workbench, on a terrace or in a car, the gap between men can shrink to a few centimetres without anyone noticing.

The chapter on proxemics described how angle changes what a distance means, and the opening chapter of this part described why side by side suits so many men. Closeness side by side asks for nothing: there is no face to hold, no eye contact to manage, no question of what the closeness means. Face to face, the same distance becomes intense, whether as intimacy or as confrontation.

This has practical uses. If you want to be near a man who is struggling, sit beside him rather than in front of him. If two men are squaring up face to face, getting one of them to turn so that they stand side by side, looking at the same thing, can lower the temperature before a word is said. And if you want to talk to a man about something that matters, arrange to be shoulder to shoulder, not nose to nose.

The figures here work side by side at a bench, close enough that their elbows nearly touch. Facing each other across the same distance, they would feel the need to step back. Side by side, neither notices.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men tolerated the same distance face to face as side by side. Angle effects on comfortable distance are well established in proxemics research, though their size varies between people and cultures.

teach.p:
Because the normal gap between men is stable, changes in it are informative. When a man moves closer than usual, the rivals include warmth and trust, especially after a shared experience or a confidence; the wish to say something private; the effects of alcohol, which loosens spacing as the chapter on substance use described; and challenge. A man who closes distance face to face, chest forward, chin up, is often squaring up, which the chapter on disagreement takes up later.

When a man moves further away than usual, the rivals include discomfort with the subject, disagreement, a wish to leave, embarrassment after something has been said, and simple respect, such as giving someone room when they are upset. A friend who steps back when you put a hand on his shoulder is telling you something about that moment, not necessarily about you.

Read the change against his baseline, and alongside other channels. Distance plus a turned torso and folded arms says something different from distance plus an open stance and steady eye contact. And remember the settings that change the rules: a crowd, a team, a funeral, a bar.

The figures here show one of the plainest changes: one man leaning in, the other leaning back, turning away and folding his arms. Whatever the words between them, the bodies are negotiating distance, and the man leaning in has a choice about whether to notice.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if changes in the distance between two men carried no information about their state or relationship. Proxemics research shows that they do, but always ambiguously, which is why rivals must be considered.

teach.p:
None of this means that men should stand closer together, or that distance is a problem to be fixed. Many men are comfortable with their spacing, and the chapter on proxemics made the central rule clear: let the other person set the distance. But it is worth noticing how much closeness men deny themselves and each other out of fear of what it might mean.

Some practical steps follow. Offer closeness through a shared focus, side by side, rather than face to face. When a friend is struggling, sit beside him, and let a hand on the shoulder or a shoulder against his do some of the work, if he welcomes it. Do not police other men's closeness with jokes about what it means; those jokes are how the fear is passed on, especially to boys who are watching. If you are a father, the way you stand with your own friends teaches your son what is allowed.

Be equally careful in the other direction. Closeness that a man has not chosen, from a boss, a coach or a stranger, can be just as uncomfortable as distance, and for some men, including those with experiences of violence described in the chapter on trauma, much more so.

The figures here stand together, one with a hand resting on the other's shoulder while he bows his head. It is a small closing of the gap, offered and accepted. For many men, it is as close as they will come to another man in a year, and it may be enough.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men who wanted more closeness with other men faced no social cost for it. The research on homohysteria suggests that the cost is real but falling in some places, so how much room there is depends on where and among whom you live.

poseGallery.doCaption: Shoulder to shoulder on a bench
poseGallery.annotation: The same distance that feels like a challenge face to face feels like company side by side.
Face to face at close range raises the temperature. Turning to an angle gives both men room without anyone stepping back.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Backing away from a friend's comfort
poseGallery.annotation: A hand on the shoulder asks for nothing. If you can, let it stay a moment; if you cannot, step back gently and say so.

poseGallery.doCaption: Side by side, an arm round him if he wants it
poseGallery.dontCaption: Keeping a careful gap from a grieving friend
poseGallery.annotation: The usual gap between men can feel like a wall at the wrong moment. Offer closeness from the side, and let him take as much as he wants.

poseGallery.doCaption: Sitting beside him, a hand's width apart
poseGallery.dontCaption: Taking the far end of the bench, arms crossed
poseGallery.annotation: In a shared crisis, the usual distance can shrink. Moving along a bench, side by side, is an offer that is easy to accept or decline.

poseGallery.doCaption: Letting friends stand as close as they like
poseGallery.dontCaption: A joke that polices two men's closeness
poseGallery.annotation: Jokes like "get a room" teach boys that closeness between men will be laughed at. Not laughing, and saying so lightly, can change that.

caseStudy:
Tom, fifty-eight, has never been a man for closeness. He shakes hands with his friends, keeps an arm's length at the pub, and once told his son Ryan, then ten, that men do not sit on each other's laps. At Tom's retirement party, Ryan, now twenty-seven, arrives with three friends who greet each other with long hugs, lean on each other at the bar and sit squashed together on a sofa. Tom feels a flicker of disapproval and then, unexpectedly, something closer to envy.

When Ryan hugs him goodbye, Tom stiffens and pats him twice on the back. Ryan notices, and lets go quickly.

A month later they go to a match together, standing on the terrace for the first time in years. In the eighty-ninth minute their team scores, and Tom finds that he has grabbed Ryan around the shoulders and is shouting into his ear. Neither of them mentions it. On the walk back to the car they are closer than they have been for years, elbows bumping.

In the pub afterwards, Tom tells Ryan about his own father, who never touched him except to shake his hand on his wedding day. Ryan listens, side by side at the bar. He does not make a joke of it.

At Christmas, when Ryan arrives, Tom hugs him first, a little awkwardly, and holds on a moment longer than a back slap would allow. Ryan's friends would not have noticed anything unusual about it. Tom notices for the rest of the day.
observe: Notice the distance men keep from each other in a queue, a waiting room or a bar, and compare it with other pairs nearby.
Notice settings where men stand much closer together, such as a team, a crowd or a funeral, and what licenses the closeness.
Notice how close you stand to male friends face to face and side by side, and whether the difference surprises you.
Notice any joke or comment that polices closeness between men, and how the men involved respond.

drills.name: Distance Map
steps: List five men you see regularly: a friend, a colleague, a relative, an acquaintance, someone you admire.
For each, estimate how far apart you usually stand or sit, face to face and side by side.
Note any settings where the distance changes, such as sport, drink or grief.
Mark any relationship where you would like the distance to be different.
Write one sentence about what the map shows you.
variations: Do the map for women you see regularly as well, and compare the distances with those you keep with men.
Ask one friend how close he thinks you usually stand, and compare his estimate with yours.

drills.name: Angle Experiment
steps: Next time you talk with a male friend standing face to face, notice the distance you keep.
Later in the conversation, shift so that you are side by side, looking at the same thing.
Notice whether the distance between you changes without either of you deciding it.
Afterwards, note any difference in how the conversation felt.
variations: Try the experiment walking side by side rather than standing, and notice how close you end up without thinking.
Try sitting at a corner of a table rather than across it, and notice the effect on distance and conversation.

drills.name: The Joke That Polices
steps: Recall a time when a joke or remark made closeness between two men seem suspect or ridiculous.
Write down what was said and how the men reacted.
Write what the joke was teaching anyone who heard it, including any boys present.
Write a sentence you could say, lightly, if you hear a joke like it again.
variations: Notice the next joke of this kind you hear, and how the people it was aimed at responded in the minutes afterwards.
Practise your sentence aloud, in a light, friendly tone, so that it is ready when you need it.

drills.name: Read the Change
steps: Over a week, watch for moments when a man you know moves noticeably closer or further away than usual.
For each, write the rival explanations: warmth, privacy, alcohol, challenge, discomfort, disagreement, respect.
Note the other channels: torso, arms, face, voice.
Where appropriate, check your reading with a question, and record whether you were right.
variations: Ask one person, gently, about a change in distance you noticed, such as "You sat right next to me today. All right?"
Watch for changes in your own distance from people over a week, and what lay behind each one.

quiz.q: Two old friends stand an arm's length apart while talking at a party, further apart than two women nearby who have just met. What does this chapter suggest?
options: The two men are probably not as close as they claim to be
The distance shows that they are quietly in disagreement
The gap often reflects norms for men, not how close they are
One of the men is probably uncomfortable with the other
quiz.explain: Distance between men is often larger than between women whatever the friendship, and gender roles seem to explain more of it than sex. Read distance against what is normal for those men in that setting.

quiz.q: What did Novelli, Drury and Reicher find when people arranged chairs for a conversation?
options: People placed their chairs further from members of their own group
People sat closer to someone presented as a member of their own group
The number of people in the room was the only thing that mattered
People sat closest to strangers whose group they did not know
quiz.explain: Personal space shrank when the other person was presented as one of us. Shared identity, rather than crowding as such, changed how close people were willing to be.

quiz.q: What does Eric Anderson's term homohysteria refer to?
options: Men's fear of being seen as gay, which leads them to police closeness
The anxiety that gay men feel when entering male-dominated spaces
A clinical condition involving panic in crowded public places
The excitement shared by fans when their team scores a late goal
quiz.explain: Anderson used the term for straight men's fear of being thought gay, which he argued drives avoidance of closeness, touch and tenderness between men. He and McCormack described this fear as declining among some younger men.

quiz.q: What did the 1976 lavatory study by Middlemist and colleagues find, and why is it also taught as a warning?
options: Closeness made no difference, and the study was a model of ethical care
Men urinated faster when another man stood nearby, without consent
Men refused to use urinals at all once they knew they were observed
A nearby man delayed urination, and the men were watched in secret
quiz.explain: The closer another man stood, the longer the delay before urinating, which suggests that closeness raises arousal. The men were observed through a periscope without consent or debriefing, which is why the study is used as an ethics example.

quiz.q: Two men are squaring up face to face in a pub, chests forward. You know one of them. What fits this chapter best?
options: Step between them face to face and tell them both to calm down
Get your friend to turn and stand beside you, facing the bar
Move closer to the other man so that he knows you are involved
Stay at a distance and wait to see whether anything happens
quiz.explain: Turning someone from face to face to side by side lowers the intensity of a close distance without anyone having to step back. De-escalation in depth belongs to Part VI, but changing the angle is often a good first move.

quiz.q: A friend who usually keeps his distance steps in close while telling you his marriage is in trouble. What is the best reading?
options: He is probably drunk, since he never usually stands this close
He is challenging you and wants you to step back and give way
He is uncomfortable and wants you to end the conversation now
The closeness may be trust and privacy; read it with the rest
quiz.explain: A move closer can mean warmth, privacy, alcohol or challenge. In this context, trust and the wish to speak privately are the likeliest rivals, but the other channels and his baseline should guide the reading.

quiz.q: In Uzzell and Horne's 2006 study, what mattered more than biological sex for the distances people kept?
options: How strongly people identified with traditionally masculine or feminine traits
How tall each person was, since taller people always need more personal space
How many brothers and sisters each person had grown up with in the family home
The time of day, since everyone stands further apart in the afternoons than mornings
quiz.explain: Gender role, how strongly people identified with masculine or feminine traits, predicted distance better than whether they were male or female. Men's spacing is partly a performance of a certain kind of masculinity.

quiz.q: A new colleague from Brazil stands closer than you are used to, touches your arm as he talks, and follows when you step back. What fits this chapter best?
options: Avoid him, since his behaviour shows that he does not respect your space
Report him to human resources at once for inappropriate physical contact
Read it as a different spacing norm, and say kindly what feels comfortable
Copy him exactly, standing even closer, so that he learns how it feels
quiz.explain: Spacing norms vary across cultures, and a step back met by a step forward is a classic sign of two norms meeting. Understanding the difference, and saying kindly what you prefer, works better than avoidance.

quiz.q: Someone says that young men today are all comfortable with physical closeness, so the old rules no longer apply. What does this chapter say?
options: It is right, since research shows the old norms have vanished completely
Research on some groups found change; it does not apply to every young man
It is wrong, since young men today keep more distance than any generation
It is right for young men in cities, though rural men have not changed at all
quiz.explain: Anderson and McCormack described more affection among some groups of young men, but the research is based on particular settings and its reach has been questioned. Read the individual, not the generation.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific man in your life with whom you keep more distance than you would like, or less than he would like. Describe how close you usually stand or sit, in which settings the distance changes, and where you think your rules about closeness between men came from: a father, school, sport, a culture. What would one small step toward the closeness you want look like, and what would make it easier for both of you?
reflection.guidance: Be specific about the rule and where you learned it: a remark, a joke, a moment when someone pulled away from you or you pulled away from them. A small step is enough, such as sitting beside him rather than opposite, or letting a hand on the shoulder stay. If closeness from men is difficult for reasons of past harm, honour that, and do not push yourself.

failureMode: The first failure is to read the larger gap between men as coldness, when it usually reflects norms rather than feeling. The second is to ignore the force behind many of those norms, the fear of being seen as gay, and to keep passing it on through jokes and comments that boys and other men absorb. The third is to read a change in distance as one thing, warmth or challenge, without weighing the rivals and the other channels. The fourth is to impose closeness, from a position of power or on someone for whom it is unwelcome. And the fifth is to forget angle: offering closeness face to face when shoulder to shoulder would have been easy for both of you.

moreCases.title: The friend who sat too close
moreCases.scene:
Owen, thirty, and Rhys, thirty-one, share a flat and have been friends since university. They have a routine on Sunday evenings: Owen at
  one end of the sofa, Rhys in the armchair, a film on. One Sunday, Rhys comes in, ignores the armchair and sits on the sofa right next to Owen,
  their shoulders almost touching, though the other end of the sofa is empty. He does not say anything. He watches the film, quietly, and does
  not make his usual jokes.

  Owen feels a flash of awkwardness. He shifts a few centimetres along the sofa and makes a joke about Rhys needing his own space. Rhys laughs,
  briefly, and moves back to the armchair. Halfway through the film, he says he is tired and goes to bed.

  The next morning, Owen learns from a mutual friend that Rhys's girlfriend ended their four-year relationship on Saturday night.

Rhys had not told Owen because he did not know how to say it. He had come home, seen Owen on the sofa, and simply wanted to be near someone. He told Owen later that he had been about to say something when Owen moved along.

Looking back, Owen also remembers that Rhys had not eaten dinner, which was unusual, and that he had left his phone face down on the kitchen counter rather than carrying it everywhere, as he normally did. At the time, none of it registered. It was just a quiet Sunday.
moreCases.misread:
Owen read Rhys's sudden closeness as odd, something to be joked away, because it broke the rules they had always kept. He did not ask what had changed, or consider that the move along the sofa might have been a request.

And because they had kept the same spacing for years, the change felt to Owen like a breach of an agreement, when it was the most honest thing Rhys could manage that night.

The joke about needing space was also a way of naming the closeness so that it could be laughed off. It is one of the most common ways men handle a moment that feels too intimate, and one of the most effective at ending it.
moreCases.betterRead:
Because the normal gap between men is stable, a change in it is informative. When a man moves closer than usual, the rivals this chapter lists include warmth and trust, the wish to say something private, alcohol and challenge. A friend who sits closer than usual, quietly, without his usual jokes, on the day after a loss, is often asking for company without words. Owen's move along the sofa and his joke were the policing of closeness that this chapter describes, done almost by reflex, and they told Rhys that the request had been refused. A better reading would have noticed the whole cluster, the closeness, the quiet and the missing jokes, and stayed put. A simple "You all right, mate?" would have opened the door. Owen went and knocked on Rhys's door the next evening, apologised for the joke, and asked how he was. Rhys told him. The following Sunday, Owen sat in the middle of the sofa, and Rhys sat beside him.

He also noticed, afterwards, how quickly his joke had come. It was not a decision. It was a habit, learned long ago, and he was surprised to find it in himself.

moreCases.title: The joke on the touchline
moreCases.scene:
Dave coaches an under-fourteens rugby team. After a hard-fought win, the boys pile into each other on the pitch: hugging, arms round
  shoulders, two of them lifting a third onto their shoulders. On the touchline, one of the fathers, Gary, laughs loudly and shouts, "Get a room,
  lads!" A couple of other fathers laugh too.

  Dave watches the boys. Several of them let go of each other at once. Two who had been hugging step apart and start messing about with the ball,
  looking embarrassed. One of the youngest, Ethan, who has been hugging his best friend after scoring his first try, goes red and walks off to the
  changing room on his own.

  Dave has seen this happen before. He also remembers his own father saying the same kind of thing when he was a boy.

Gary is not a bad man. He drives three of the boys to every away match and has never missed a training session. He would be shocked to be told that his joke had sent a thirteen-year-old off the pitch on his own.

Ethan's mother, who had been standing a little further along the touchline, saw her son walk off and followed him to the changing room. She found him sitting on a bench, still in his kit, not crying, but very quiet. When she asked what was wrong, he said nothing was, and that he did not want to play next week.
moreCases.misread:
Gary read the boys' hugs as something faintly ridiculous, and his joke as harmless banter. The boys read the joke clearly: closeness between them was being watched, and laughed at, by the men they looked up to.

The other fathers' laughter mattered as much as the joke. A single remark can be shrugged off; a group of men laughing tells the boys that this is what men think.

It also missed what the boys' closeness was for: celebrating together after a hard match, which is exactly what teams are supposed to do.
moreCases.betterRead:
Eric Anderson's term homohysteria describes men's fear of being seen as gay, and how it leads them to police their own closeness and each other's. Anderson and Mark McCormack have described younger men being more comfortable with hugging and physical affection than earlier generations, though their research comes from particular groups. A joke like Gary's shows how the old rules are passed on: not by explanation, but by laughter at the moment of closeness, which teaches boys to step apart. Dave's better response was to address it, lightly but clearly, without shaming Gary in public. He walked over and said, with a smile, "They've just won a hard match. Let them enjoy it." Later, he spoke to Gary privately. In the changing room, he made a point of hugging Ethan and congratulating him on his try, in front of the team. The next week, after the match, the boys hugged again. Gary kept quiet.

He also mentioned it to the club's welfare officer, who added a short line about touchline behaviour to the parents' code of conduct for the next season.

moreCases.title: The colleague who stood too close
moreCases.scene:
Rafael, thirty-four, has moved from São Paulo to a software company in Manchester. He is warm, talkative and quickly popular. But his
  colleague Steve, forty-five, finds him hard to be around. When they talk, Rafael stands closer than Steve is used to, often touches his arm or
  shoulder, and holds his gaze for longer. Steve keeps backing away. In one conversation by the coffee machine, he takes three steps back, and Rafael
  follows, until Steve is almost against the wall.

  Steve starts avoiding Rafael, eating lunch at his desk and answering his questions by message. Rafael notices and is hurt. He tells another
  colleague that Steve seems cold, maybe even unfriendly towards foreigners.

  Steve, for his part, tells his wife that the new Brazilian guy is a bit full on, and that he does not know how to tell him to back off.

Rafael has also noticed that the team greet each other without touching at all, even after weekends, and has started to wonder whether he has done something to offend everyone.

Their manager has noticed the tension and asked Steve, in a one-to-one, whether everything is all right with the new hire. Steve said it was fine. He did not want to seem like the man who could not cope with a friendly colleague, and he could not quite say what the problem was.
moreCases.misread:
Each read the other through his own spacing norms. Steve read Rafael's closeness and touch as pushiness, and Rafael read Steve's backing away as coldness or prejudice. Neither considered that the other was simply standing where his own culture told him to.

And Rafael's reading, that Steve might dislike foreigners, was the kind of conclusion people reach when a cultural difference is not named: the other person's behaviour is explained by their character rather than their norms.

They also each told someone else their reading of the other, rather than telling each other, which is how cultural misreadings harden into reputations.
moreCases.betterRead:
The chapter on proxemics described how preferred distances vary across cultures, and Brazil is often described as a culture where friendly conversation involves closer distances and more touch than in northern England. Rafael was being warm in his own dialect; Steve was being polite in his. The dance by the coffee machine, one man stepping back and the other following, is a classic sign of two spacing norms meeting. Neither man was wrong. The better approach was for each to understand the other's norm and for Steve, who was uncomfortable, to say so kindly. A colleague who knew them both suggested it. Steve said to Rafael, over a coffee, "I'm a bit of a space person, I'm afraid. Very English. It's nothing personal." Rafael laughed and said that in Brazil people would think Steve was angry with him. They found a middle distance. Steve started eating lunch with the team again, and Rafael learned to save his hugs for Fridays.

Steve also admitted to his wife that he had been relieved to find Rafael so easy to talk to about it.

moreCases.title: Squared up at the bar
moreCases.scene:
Late on a Saturday night, in a busy pub, Josh notices his friend Kieran in a conversation at the bar with a man he does not know. At first
  they are standing at a normal distance, angled, talking about the match on the television. Then something changes. The stranger turns square on
  to Kieran and steps forward, closing the gap to half a metre. His chest is pushed forward, his chin up, his arms slightly away from his body.
  Kieran turns to face him too, and does not step back. Their voices get louder.

  Josh's other friend, Liam, says to leave them to it, that Kieran can look after himself. Someone else nearby has started filming on a phone.

  Josh has seen Kieran in a fight once, years ago, and he remembers how quickly it happened.

Kieran has had four pints, and his team lost that afternoon. The stranger has had at least as many. Josh can see the landlord at the far end of the bar, watching, one hand already near the phone.

Josh also notices that the stranger's two friends have stopped talking and are watching, one of them putting his drink down on the bar. Kieran's hands have closed into fists at his sides, and his face, which was flushed from the drink, has gone suddenly pale.
moreCases.misread:
Liam read the change in distance as a private matter between two grown men. The filming bystander read it as entertainment. Neither reading took seriously what the change in distance and posture meant.

The phone being raised also mattered. An audience makes it harder for either man to back down, because backing down now happens in front of everyone and possibly online.

Liam's reading also assumed that what mattered was Kieran's ability to look after himself, when the real question was whether anyone would get hurt, including people standing nearby.

The stranger's friends going quiet and putting their drinks down was also a sign Liam missed: the people closest to the stranger were reading the same change Josh was.
moreCases.betterRead:
A man who closes the distance face to face, chest forward, chin up, arms away from his body, is often squaring up, one of the rivals this chapter lists for a sudden change in distance, and the one that matters most for safety. When two men do it to each other, their ladders, in the terms of the chapter on anger, are climbing together. The better reading was to act early, before either man reached the top. Josh walked over, did not get between them face to face, and came in at an angle beside Kieran. He said, easily, "Kieran, mate, our taxi's here," and put a hand on his shoulder, turning him gently towards the door. To the stranger, he said, "Sorry, mate, we've got to go." The angle and the exit gave both men a way out without either backing down in front of the other. Outside, Kieran said the man had insulted his team and that he would have flattened him. Josh said he knew, and that was why they had left.

Josh noted afterwards that the gap between the two men had told him what was coming before their voices did.

workedReading.title: The bench in the waiting room
workedReading.scene:
Mark, forty, sits in a hospital relatives' room waiting for news of his mother, who has had a stroke. His father, Ken, seventy-two, sits at the far end of the same long bench, two metres away. They have never been close. Ken was a stern, distant father, and in the past ten years they have spoken mostly at Christmas. Ken sits upright, his hands gripped together between his knees, staring at the floor. His jaw is tight and he has not spoken for twenty minutes. Mark wants to move closer, and does not know whether he should.

The relatives' room is small, overheated and lit by fluorescent tubes. A television on the wall is showing the news with the sound off. The only other person in the room, a woman in her sixties, is crying quietly into a tissue by the door.

Mark's mother has always been the bridge between them. Whatever he and his father have needed to say to each other, she has said for them. Sitting in the relatives' room, Mark realises that if she does not recover, there will be nobody to say it.

steps.label: Notice the gap
steps.text:
Mark notices the distance between them: the far end of the bench, two metres, with the whole bench empty in between. He notes that this is how he and his father have always sat: in cars, at dinner, at the funeral of Ken's brother. The gap is their baseline, not a new message.

He also notices that he chose his own seat when he came in, at the opposite end, without thinking. The gap is something they both keep, not something his father imposes.

He also notes that there is nobody else to sit with. The usual buffers, his mother, his wife, the television, are not here, and for once the two of them have only each other.

steps.label: Read the rest of the body
steps.text:
He looks at the rest of his father's body. The hands gripped between the knees, the upright, braced posture, the jaw and the stare at the floor fit a man holding himself together in fear, not a man who wants to be left alone in anger. His father is not turned away from him. He is simply not turned towards anyone.

He also notices his father's shoes, polished as always, and his tie, which he has put on to come to the hospital. Ken has dressed for an occasion. It is the closest he comes to showing how serious he thinks this is.

He also notes that his father's knee is bouncing slightly, which he has never seen before. Ken is a still man by nature. The movement is a pacifier, and it tells Mark how frightened he is.

steps.label: Consider the situation
steps.text:
This is one of the settings where the usual rules change. A shared crisis, like a shared crowd, can shrink the gap between people, as Novelli, Drury and Reicher found when people felt part of the same group. Mark and his father are, for once, on the same side of something. That makes closeness more possible than it has been for years.

He also remembers that the only time his father has ever hugged him was at his grandmother's funeral, briefly, at the graveside. Crises, for Ken, have been the only times the rules relaxed.

He also knows that his father served in the army in his twenties, and that he has always found hospitals difficult, though he has never said why.

steps.label: Hold the rivals open
steps.text:
His father might want company and not know how to ask. He might want to be left alone with his fear. He might find closeness from his son, after years of distance, unbearable at this moment. Mark notes that he cannot tell which, and that the safest offer is a small one that his father can easily decline.

He also considers his own feelings. He wants closeness partly for himself: he is frightened too. He notes that this is fine, and that it is one more reason to make the offer small enough for his father to refuse without either of them feeling rejected.

He also reminds himself that a refusal would not be a rejection of him. A man who has kept his distance for seventy years may simply not know how to do anything else in a moment like this.

steps.label: Offer closeness side by side
steps.text:
Mark does not go and sit opposite his father or crouch in front of him, which would put them face to face. He moves along the bench to the middle, about an arm's length from Ken, and sits as his father sits, looking at the floor. He says, quietly, "Do you want a tea, Dad?" It is an offer that has nothing to do with feelings, side by side, with a natural yes or no.

He chooses an arm's length deliberately. Close enough to be beside him, far enough not to crowd him. The middle of the bench is an offer, not a claim.

He also keeps his eyes on the same patch of floor as his father. Looking at the same thing, as the opening chapter of this part described, can bring two people together without either having to look at the other.

steps.label: Let him set the distance
steps.text:
Ken says no, and then, after a long pause, "Thanks, son." He does not move away. A few minutes later, he shifts slightly along the bench, closing a little of the gap, and says that he keeps thinking about how she looked when the ambulance came. Mark says that it must have been terrifying. Ken nods, and keeps looking at the floor.

He also resists the urge to say more. The closing of the gap is doing the talking, and words about it might make his father self-conscious and send him back to the end of the bench.

He also notices that his father's hands have loosened slightly since he sat down nearer, and that his breathing has become a little slower. Small changes, but ones Mark has not seen in him before.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
When the doctor comes in to say that his mother is stable and will be moved to a ward, Ken's shoulders drop and he lets out a long breath. Then he puts his hand on Mark's shoulder and leaves it there for a moment, which he has not done since Mark was a boy. Mark does not say anything about it. He notes that the gap between them on the bench, two metres at the start and half a metre at the end, had said more about the evening than anything either of them had managed to say aloud.

On the way to the ward, they walk side by side down the corridor, and Ken says, without looking at him, that he is glad Mark came. Mark says he is glad too.

Mark also tells his wife about the bench that night, and she says that it is the first time in ten years she has heard him talk about his father without bitterness. He visits his parents more often after that, and sits beside his father in the garden.

moreFailures.title: Reading the gap as coldness
moreFailures.body:
Two men who stand an arm's length apart, angle themselves away from each other and leave an empty seat between them may be very close friends. In many cultures, that is simply how men stand. Uzzell and Horne's research found that gender role mattered more than biological sex for the distances people kept, which suggests that men's spacing is partly a performance of a certain kind of masculinity rather than a measure of feeling. Read the distance between two men against what is normal for those men, in that setting and that culture, not against what would be normal between women, or between other men somewhere else.

It also helps to remember that distance changes with age, setting and familiarity. Two men who stand apart in their twenties may sit together on a bench in their seventies; the norms soften for many men as they age.

It also helps to remember that men may be closer in private than in public. Two friends who keep an arm's length at the pub may sit side by side on the sofa at home, talking for hours. Public spacing is partly for the audience.

It also helps to watch how men use objects to manage the gap: a pint held between them, a phone, a table, a dog on a lead. These give two men something to look at and hold, and make distance feel natural rather than awkward.

moreFailures.title: Passing on the policing
moreFailures.body:
Much of men's careful spacing is maintained by jokes and remarks that make closeness between men seem suspect: "Get a room", "Are you two married?", "Steady on". Each one is usually meant as harmless banter, and each one teaches anyone listening, especially boys, that closeness between men will be watched and laughed at. They also make gay men targets, and they keep straight men from comfort they might want. You do not need to lecture anyone. Noticing the joke, not laughing, and saying something light, such as "Let them enjoy it," is often enough to change what a group of boys learns.

Adults sometimes police girls' and women's closeness too, but the pressure on boys and men is often sharper, and the consequences for boys who do not conform can be severe.

Parents can also pass it on without jokes, through what they praise and discourage. A father who tells his son that men shake hands, not hug, is setting the same rule in a kinder voice.

Sports clubs, schools and youth groups have a particular chance to change this. Coaches and teachers who treat affection between boys as normal, and who do not laugh at jokes that police it, can shape what a whole team learns.

moreFailures.title: Reading a change in distance as one thing
moreFailures.body:
When a man moves closer than usual, it is tempting to settle on one reading: he is being warm, or he is being aggressive. The rivals in this chapter matter. A friend who sits closer after a loss is often asking for company. A man who steps in at a bar may be friendly, drunk or squaring up. A colleague from another culture may simply be standing where his culture puts people. Read the change alongside the rest of the body, the torso, chest, chin, arms, face and voice, and alongside what has just happened, before you decide what it means.

It also helps to watch your own reaction. A flash of discomfort when a man moves closer is information about your norms, not necessarily about his intent, and it is worth noticing before you act on it.

It also helps to watch for the moment when a change in distance is followed by a change in voice. A man who moves closer and lowers his voice is usually confiding; a man who moves closer and raises it is usually not.

moreFailures.title: Imposing closeness
moreFailures.body:
Once men notice how much closeness they deny themselves, some decide to fix it by moving in: standing closer, sitting beside, putting an arm round a friend's shoulders. Done with care, this can be welcome. Done without reading the other person, it overrides his right to set his own distance, which the chapter on proxemics made the central rule. Some men are comfortable with more space; some have reasons, from past experiences, culture or sensory sensitivity, to prefer it. Offer closeness, side by side and lightly, and let the other person decide how much of it to take.

It also helps to remember that touch and closeness carry different weight for people with experience of abuse or violence. The chapter on trauma described how an unexpected approach can set off an alarm. Moving slowly and from the side respects that.

It also helps to watch what happens after you offer closeness. If the other person relaxes, stays or moves closer, the offer was welcome. If he stiffens, turns or edges away, step back without comment.

And remember that closeness can be offered in other ways than distance: a message, a call, a shared task, an invitation. Not every offer of closeness needs to be physical.

questions.q: Why do men leave an empty seat between them?
questions.a:
Partly because of the norms that this chapter describes. In many cultures, two men sitting right next to each other when there is space to spread out can feel too intimate, or can be read by others as a sign of a romantic relationship, and the fear of that reading, what Eric Anderson called homohysteria, shapes how men arrange themselves. Partly, too, because people in general tend to spread out when they can, to protect their own space. The empty seat is rarely about dislike. Two close friends at the cinema may leave it, and then share popcorn across it all evening.

It also helps to notice when the seat is filled. Two men who sit right next to each other at the cinema, with space available, are telling you something about their relationship, or about how they feel that night.

It also helps to know that women sometimes leave a gap too, especially with strangers, and that men sometimes do not. The empty seat is a tendency, not a law.

questions.q: Are younger men really more comfortable with closeness?
questions.a:
Some research suggests that many are. Anderson and McCormack described boys and young men in British schools, universities and sports teams hugging, cuddling and expressing affection for each other in ways that, they argued, would have been unusual a generation earlier. But their research is mostly qualitative and based on particular groups, and some researchers have questioned how widely the change applies, especially outside middle-class and white settings. The safest reading is that norms are shifting in some places and among some young men, and that you should not assume any individual, young or old, follows the pattern.

It also helps to notice your own generation's rules. A father who was taught to keep his distance from other men may find his son's hugs strange, and it is worth asking whether the strangeness is about the hugs or about what he was taught.

It also helps to watch how different generations within one family handle closeness. Grandfathers, fathers and sons often follow different rules, and noticing the differences can make it easier to talk about them.

questions.q: Is it wrong to want more space than other people?
questions.a:
No. People differ in how much space they need, and the right to set your own distance is the central rule of the chapter on proxemics. Some men simply prefer more space; some have sensory sensitivities, past experiences or cultural habits that make closeness uncomfortable. The point of this chapter is not that men should stand closer, but that they should understand why they stand where they do, and notice when the gap is protecting them from comfort they might actually want. If you prefer space, it can help to say so kindly, as Steve did, so that others do not read it as coldness.

It also helps to know that space preferences can be temporary. Someone who is tired, unwell, overwhelmed or upset may want more room than usual, and less on a good day.

It may also help to explain your preference before it becomes a problem. A new colleague or a new friend who knows you like space is much less likely to take your distance personally.

It also helps to know that space needs can be different at home and at work, and with friends and strangers. A man who likes a lot of room at the office may be very comfortable close to his partner or his children.

questions.q: Why can men stand so close together at football?
questions.a:
Because shared identity changes the rules. Novelli, Drury and Reicher found that people placed their chairs closer to someone they believed was a member of their own group, and that crowds people feel part of are experienced very differently from crowds of strangers. On a terrace, singing, celebrating a goal, men are part of something larger, and the usual fear of what closeness might mean recedes. The same men who keep a careful gap at a bus stop will hug strangers when their team scores. The setting gives permission that ordinary life does not.

The same effect can be seen at concerts, protests, festivals and religious gatherings, where people who feel part of a group often tolerate, and even enjoy, a closeness they would avoid among strangers.

Shared grief can do the same. At funerals, men who would never touch each other otherwise often stand shoulder to shoulder, put an arm round each other, or hold each other up.

questions.q: How should I respond if a friend moves closer than usual?
questions.a:
Look at the rest of the picture first. If he is quiet, low, or has just had bad news, the move is probably a request for company, and the kindest response is to stay where you are, perhaps ask how he is, and let the closeness be. If he has been drinking, it may mean little. If his chest is forward, his chin up and his voice rising, it may be a challenge, and the chapter on anger describes what to do. If you are not sure, a simple, warm question, "You all right, mate?", is almost always a safe first step, and it lets him tell you what the move meant.

It also helps to let the closeness be ordinary. Commenting on it, such as "You're very cuddly tonight," can make a man self-conscious and send him back to his usual distance.

It also helps to notice whether he moves away again. A friend who moves close for a few minutes and then returns to his usual distance may have said what he needed to, and the return is not a rejection.

It also helps to remember that your own reaction may be visible. If you shift away when a friend moves closer, he will probably see it, and may not try again for a long time.

questions.q: Why is the urinal study taught as a warning?
questions.a:
Because of how it was done. In 1976, Dennis Middlemist and colleagues observed men in a university lavatory through a periscope in a cubicle, measuring how long it took them to begin urinating with another man at different distances. The men did not consent and were not told afterwards, and the study was criticised at the time as an invasion of privacy and dignity. It found that closeness delayed urination, which the authors took as evidence that crowding raises physical arousal. This book keeps both lessons: closeness between men has real physical effects, and curiosity about other people's bodies has limits that no research question overrides.

Today, research of this kind would have to pass an ethics review, and covert observation of people in toilets would almost certainly not be allowed.

The lesson for readers is the same as in the chapter on the ethics of reading people: watching others is never a licence to intrude on them, however interesting the question.

watch.title: Invading personal space in public
watch.notice: Strangers have their personal space invaded in everyday places. Watch the reactions: leaning away, turning the shoulders, blocking with bags, moving off, often without a word.

reviewPrompt: This week, notice the distance you keep from three men face to face and side by side, and try sitting beside one of them instead of opposite.
